01

What Seaborn is — and how it sits on Matplotlib

Seaborn is a statistical plotting library built on top of Matplotlib. It doesn't replace anything you've learned — every Seaborn chart is a Matplotlib Figure and Axes underneath. What Seaborn adds is a higher-level vocabulary: you describe what the data means ("color by smoker, split by day"), and it handles the grouping, aggregation, colors, and legend for you.

The plotting stack
Seaborn — statistical charts, themes, palettes
↓
Matplotlib — Figure, Axes, artists
↓
NumPy & Pandas — the data
↓
Your screen or image file

Install and import

pip install seaborn
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print(sns.__version__)

sns is the universal alias — the joke is that it's the initials of Samuel Norman Seaborn, a character from The West Wing. You still import matplotlib.pyplot, because you'll use it for plt.show(), titles, saving files, and anything Seaborn doesn't cover.

The same chart, two ways

Here is a grouped comparison — average tip by day, split by whether the party smoked — first in pure Matplotlib, then in Seaborn:

# Matplotlib: you do the grouping, positioning, and legend yourself
means = tips.groupby(["day", "smoker"])["tip"].mean().unstack()
means.plot(kind="bar")

# Seaborn: describe the chart, it does the rest
sns.barplot(data=tips, x="day", y="tip", hue="smoker")
The trade Seaborn gives up some low-level control in exchange for speed and sensible defaults. And because it returns a normal Matplotlib Axes, you never get stuck — anything Seaborn can't do, you finish with the Matplotlib tools from your earlier modules.

Built-in practice datasets

Seaborn ships loaders for small example datasets, which is why almost every Seaborn tutorial starts the same way: 

tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")
print(tips.head())

print(sns.get_dataset_names())   # every dataset available
Needs internet load_dataset() downloads the file from Seaborn's GitHub repository the first time it runs, then caches it in a seaborn-data folder in your home directory. If you're offline, it will fail with a connection error — that's the network, not your code.

Working offline: load the CSV files directly

This module comes with its two datasets as plain CSV files — tips.csv and flights.csv. Save them in the same folder as your script or notebook and load them with Pandas. You get the same DataFrame, and every example in this module works unchanged: 

import pandas as pd

tips = pd.read_csv("tips.csv")          # same as sns.load_dataset("tips")
flights = pd.read_csv("flights.csv")    # same as sns.load_dataset("flights")

print(tips.shape)    # (244, 7)
print(tips.head())
Why this matters beyond practice With your own data, pd.read_csv() is what you'll actually use — load_dataset() only exists for Seaborn's built-in examples. Learning the CSV route now means the rest of the module transfers straight to real work.

02

Tidy data & the data / x / y pattern

Matplotlib asks you to pass in arrays. Seaborn asks you to pass in a DataFrame and then name the columns. That one habit — data= plus column names as strings — is the core of the whole library. 

sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip")
plt.show()

Take a look at the table behind that chart:

total_billtipsexsmokerdaytimesize
16.991.01FemaleNoSunDinner2
10.341.66MaleNoSunDinner3
21.013.50MaleNoSunDinner3

Each row is one observation (one restaurant bill). Each column is one variable. That layout is called tidy or long-form data, and it's what Seaborn is designed around.

Wide vs. long

Spreadsheets often arrive in wide form, with one column per category:

Wide

yearnorthsouth
202412095
2025140110

Long (tidy)

yearregionsales
2024north120
2024south95
2025north140
2025south110

With the long version, "region" is a column, so you can write hue="region". With the wide version there's no such column to point at. Convert wide to long with melt(): 

long_df = wide_df.melt(
    id_vars="year",          # columns to keep as they are
    var_name="region",       # new column holding the old column names
    value_name="sales"       # new column holding the values
)

sns.lineplot(data=long_df, x="year", y="sales", hue="region")
Rule of thumb If you want to say "color by ___" or "split by ___", that ___ must be a column. If it's currently spread across several column headers, you need melt() first.
📋
Tidy data
One row per observation, one column per variable.
🏷️
data=, x=, y=
Pass the DataFrame once, then refer to columns by name.
🔄
df.melt()
Reshapes wide data into the long form Seaborn prefers.
03

Your first plots — scatter, line, bar, histogram

Four functions cover a huge share of everyday charts. They all share the same data / x / y signature, so once you learn one, you've nearly learned all four.

Relationship between two numbers
sns.scatterplot()
Trend over time
sns.lineplot()
Average per category
sns.barplot()
Shape of one variable
sns.histplot()

Scatter and line

tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")    # or pd.read_csv("tips.csv")

sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip")
plt.show()

flights = sns.load_dataset("flights")   # or pd.read_csv("flights.csv")

sns.lineplot(data=flights, x="year", y="passengers")
plt.show()
Notice the shaded band The flights data has twelve rows per year (one per month). lineplot() doesn't draw twelve lines — it averages them into one line and shades a 95% confidence interval around it. Seaborn is summarizing for you, which is exactly the "statistical" in statistical plotting.

Bar and histogram

sns.barplot(data=tips, x="day", y="total_bill")    # bar height = mean per day
plt.show()

sns.histplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", bins=20, kde=True)
plt.show()

barplot() computes the average for each category and draws error bars for you. histplot() takes only an x, buckets the values into bins, and kde=True overlays a smooth density curve.

Adding a third variable with hue

The feature that makes Seaborn feel different is hue=. Name a column and Seaborn colors by it and builds the legend: 

sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="time")
plt.show()

sns.scatterplot(
    data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip",
    hue="time",       # color by lunch / dinner
    size="size",      # dot size by party size
    style="smoker"    # marker shape by smoker yes / no
)

hue, size, and style each map a column to a visual property. Use them sparingly: one is clear, two is rich, all three at once is usually noise.

Seaborn plots are Matplotlib Axes

Every function returns an Axes, and accepts ax= to draw into one you created. That's your bridge back to everything from the Matplotlib modules: 

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

sns.histplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", ax=ax1)
sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", ax=ax2)

ax1.set_title("Distribution of bills")
ax2.set_title("Bill vs. tip")
ax2.axhline(3, color="gray", linestyle="--")   # pure Matplotlib

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
A preview of Module 2 Everything in this lesson is an axes-level function — it draws on one Axes. Seaborn also has figure-level functions (relplot, displot, catplot) that build whole grids of subplots. They don't accept ax=, and we'll cover when to use each next.
⚪
scatterplot()
Two numeric variables, one dot per row.
📈
lineplot()
Trends; averages repeated x values and shades a confidence interval.
📊
barplot() / histplot()
Category averages, and the distribution of a single variable.
🎨
hue, size, style
Map extra columns to color, dot size, and marker shape.
04

Themes, contexts & color palettes

Where Matplotlib uses plt.style.use(), Seaborn has sns.set_theme() — one call that sets the background style, text scale, and color palette for every chart that follows. 

sns.set_theme(
    style="whitegrid",     # background and grid look
    context="notebook",   # overall size of text and lines
    palette="deep"        # default colors
)

sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="day")
plt.show()

Five styles

style=
darkgrid (default) whitegrid dark white ticks

whitegrid is a good choice for most reports, and ticks suits publication-style figures. To drop the top and right border lines, call sns.despine() after plotting.

Contexts: one setting for every audience

context scales labels, lines, and markers together, so the same code works for a notebook, a paper, a slide, or a poster: 

sns.set_theme(context="talk")     # paper < notebook < talk < poster

Color palettes

sns.color_palette("deep")       # the default: muted, distinct colors
sns.color_palette("pastel")     # lighter version
sns.color_palette("viridis", 5) # 5 evenly spaced colors from a colormap

sns.barplot(data=tips, x="day", y="tip", palette="pastel")
Palette previews
deep — qualitative: separate categories with no order
pastel — qualitative, softer
viridis — sequential: low to high of one numeric thing
Match the palette to the data Use a qualitative palette (deep, pastel) when hue represents categories like day or region. Use a sequential one (viridis, Blues) when it represents a number. The same idea as sequential vs. diverging colormaps from Matplotlib Module 3.
Version note In recent Seaborn versions (0.13+), passing palette= without a hue= raises a warning. If you want colored bars per category, write hue="day", palette="pastel", legend=False.
🎭
sns.set_theme()
Sets style, context, and palette for every chart after it.
📏
context=
paper, notebook, talk, poster — scales text and lines together.
🌈
palette=

✂️
sns.despine()
